extracted.intended_audience: students of political science, journalists, political leaders and campaign strategists
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for understanding how public opinion forms and how leaders/persuaders can create a common will from diverse private opinions; covers psychological conditioning, symbolic rhetoric, and practical speechcraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer specific opinions solely from economic position
rubrics_metrics.description: From Madison: differences of economic situation permit a probable difference of opinions, but you cannot infer what those opinions will necessarily be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic position may make some opinions more likely (e.g., owners resisting dispossession), but there is no fixed set of opinions attached to any economic role; analysts need special empirical inquiry rather than deterministic inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the cognitive/learned nature of self-interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary doctrine of self-interest omits the cognitive function: self and interest are 'conceived' and acquired rather than instinctive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat people's ideas of their interests as learned, variable, and conventionally shaped; avoid assuming innate or automatic conceptions of interest when explaining opinions or behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class consciousness is inducible, not automatic
rubrics_metrics.description: Socialists organize and agitate to produce 'class consciousness' because economic situation alone does not automatically produce a common conception of class interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your aim is to produce a shared class identity or political awareness, plan active organization, education, and agitation rather than relying on material conditions to create consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize instincts and dispositions are malleable through experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Instinctive acts in humans cease to be 'blind' after repetition; cognitive processes and learned associations determine what excites an instinct and how it is expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In designing persuasive appeals or educational programs, account for conditioning: the same underlying disposition (fear, pity, anger) can be attached to different stimuli and responses depending on experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'binders' or historical stereotypes to transfer positive associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Invoke widely revered names or stereotypes (e.g., 'Lincoln') as binders to transfer piety or good associations to a candidate or cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-chosen historical reference can unite disparate factions by invoking a shared, positive stereotype; ensure the binder evokes the desired, non-controversial associations for your target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open on safe subjects that avoid explosive conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Select opening subjects which will not arouse the schisms or explosive conflicts among factions, in order to establish a common mood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with non-contentious records or themes that can be accepted across factions (example: criticizing patronage) before moving to more delicate matters; this builds coalition momentum without immediate division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ ambiguous/elastic phrases to accommodate divergent interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Let words mean 'all things to all men' (e.g., 'correct principles', 'American rights', 'friendship') so different factions can read their own meanings into them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deliberately polyvalent language to assemble coalitions from groups with incompatible specific aims; this facilitates agreement under a common slogan while postponing contentious specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance specificity and thematic appeals to placate different factions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be specific on non-contentious facts but balance broad themes ('friendship' vs 'firmness') so different groups find something to endorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factual, non-explosive details to avoid arousing contrary passions, and juxtapose themes that will reassure different audiences; this helps maintain unity without alienating key subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an issue is irreconcilable, suppress or neutralize it tactically
rubrics_metrics.description: On matters that cannot be compromised (the text's example: Lusi tania), a leader may 'obliterate' the conflict by pretending it does not exist or making it a non-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a tactical move to avoid division but is risky and may be an anti-pattern if it misleads or later provokes backlash; weigh long-term costs of ignoring salient grievances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conditioned responses and transferable symbols to unite emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a symbol (e.g., 'Americanism') that can arouse the same emotion in diverse people, because the emotion is transferable across stimuli and responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design symbols that can be associated with multiple prior attachments so that emotions from disparate sources coalesce under a single emblem; the symbol need not have a precise meaning to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against 'verbalism'—names divorced from objects cause misalliances
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting names and shorthand for complex objects risks verbalism, where the name continues to be used regardless of the underlying facts and may misalign with other ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure symbolic shorthand remains tied to substantive policy or fact where possible; remind audiences occasionally of the concrete referents to avoid empty sloganeering or unintended associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affect (emotion) is immediate; cognition and conation are mediated and indirect
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea (e.g., starving child abroad) evokes immediate emotion, but the cognition of the situation and the results of actions are indirect and impersonal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Messaging that appeals to emotion can be powerful but be explicit about the limits of direct action; manage expectations about what audience actions can achieve through impersonal channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor appeals to audience variation in susceptibility to distant ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: People vary in how vividly they respond to distant or abstract stimuli; some react strongly to an idea of a distant suffering, others are almost insensitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences and choose stimuli (vivid images, local analogies, symbols) appropriate to their susceptibility; one-size-fits-all abstract appeals will not mobilize all audiences equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form coalitions around the least common denominator; vote totals mask motives
rubrics_metrics.description: A majority can be produced by uniting many different motives around a minimal shared factor (the 'least common denominator'); counting votes does not reveal the qualitative reasons behind them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume uniformity of motive from electoral outcomes; political strategy should aim to assemble overlapping incentives and symbols rather than expect a single rationale to explain mass support.
